us-declaration-of-independence: Adopted on July 4, 1776, this proclamation by the Second Continental Congress announced that the thirteen American colonies were free and independent states. It lays out the colonists’ grievances against King George III and argues that governments derive their power from the consent of the governed. The famous line — ‘all men are created equal’ — has made it one of history’s most quoted political statements.
without-prejudice: Israel Zangwill gathered his sharpest magazine writing in this essay collection from the 1890s. Best known for Children of the Ghetto, the Anglo-Jewish author turns his wit on books, plays, politics, and Jewish life in Victorian England. Readers meet a critic who could be tender and cutting in the same paragraph, and whose essays helped define how English-speaking readers saw Jewish culture at the century's end.
hypatia-or-new-foes-with-an-old-face: In fifth-century Alexandria, the brilliant philosopher Hypatia teaches astronomy and reason while her city tears itself apart. Christians and pagans clash in the streets, and she is caught between a bishop who wants her silenced and a young monk torn between faith and love. Charles Kingsley's 1853 novel dramatizes the real Hypatia's life and her famous, violent death at the hands of a mob.
public-speaking-principles-and-practice: Irvah Lester Winter wrote this practical handbook for students learning to speak in public. It covers how to build a speech, use the voice and body well, and hold an audience's attention from first word to last. Filled with exercises and examples, the guide treats speaking as a skill anyone can learn with practice — a useful manual for classrooms, clubs, and anyone facing a podium.
red-fleece: Will Levington Comfort's 1915 novel takes readers into the first months of the Great War in Europe. Through soldiers and the people caught behind the lines, it shows the shock of modern battle and the human cost measured in shattered lives. Written while the war still raged, the book carries the raw, immediate feeling of a writer trying to make sense of a catastrophe as it unfolds.
warlock-o-glenwarlock-a-homely-romance: George MacDonald, the Scottish fantasist behind beloved fairy tales, sets this novel in his native countryside. The Warlock family of Glenwarlock faces hardship and change, and the story follows their quiet struggles with MacDonald's characteristic warmth. Called a homely romance, it celebrates simple goodness, Scottish character, and the beauty of ordinary life.
the-post-office: Tagore's beloved play tells of Amal, a sick boy confined to his room who watches the world through his window and dreams of the King's postman. Through the child's imagination, the drama finds profound meaning in confinement, hope, and death. W. B. Yeats admired it deeply; its gentle wisdom has moved audiences for over a century.
the-secrets-of-the-german-war-office: Armgaard Karl Graves — self-described secret agent — exposes the workings of German military intelligence in this sensational wartime exposé. True, exaggerated, or invented, it thrilled Allied readers during the Great War. A curious and revealing document of espionage fever. It remains a vivid artifact of the spy mania that gripped nations at war.
world-s-best-histories-volume-7-france: François Guizot, the great French statesman-historian, tells the story of France — from Gaul to his own troubled age. His clear, grave narrative shaped how the world saw French history. A classic from one of history's makers. His stately narrative carries France from the ancient Gauls to modern times with wisdom and gravity.
the-dolliver-romance: Hawthorne's unfinished last romance tells of old Dr. Dolliver and his search for the elixir of life. Even incomplete, it glows with the master's autumnal magic. A precious fragment from America's greatest romancer. The old doctor's quest for life's elixir glows with Hawthorne's late, mellow art.
doctor-grimshawe-s-secret-a-romance: Hawthorne's unfinished romance of old Dr. Grimshawe and his secret — a spider, a grave, and a New England mystery — glows with his late magic. Julian Hawthorne completed the fragment with devotion. A haunting what-might-have-been. Spiders, graves, and buried gold haunt this tantalizing unfinished tale.
mornings-in-florence: John Ruskin walks readers through Florence's churches and galleries in these famous morning lessons. His passionate eye teaches us how to truly see art. The classic introduction to looking at pictures. Giotto, Ghiberti, and the great masters live again under his enthusiastic guidance.
shock-and-awe-achieving-rapid-dominance: Harlan Ullman's famous study of rapid dominance — shock and awe — argues for overwhelming force to end wars quickly. Written by a defense thinker, it shaped modern military doctrine. Controversial, influential, and still debated. Generals and scholars still argue over his bold, unsettling thesis.
horace: Theodore Martin's Horace introduces the great Roman poet — his odes, satires, and epistles — to English readers. Part of the Ancient Classics series, it wears its learning lightly. A graceful doorway into Latin poetry's most civilized voice. His Sabine farm, his friends, and his mellow wisdom charm every reader.
the-precipice: Ivan Goncharov's great novel The Precipice — his last — follows Boris Raisky, torn between art and life, amid the Russian gentry. The author's deep, slow art reaches its full power. A masterpiece of Russian realism, less known than Oblomov but equally fine.
the-albany-depot-a-farce: Howells' one-act farce The Albany Depot finds comedy in missed trains and mixed identities. Light, deft, and very funny. A small gem of American humor. Porters, passengers, and predicaments whirl through this brisk one-acter. Howells proves even a railway station can stage a comedy.
a-sicilian-romance: Ann Radcliffe's Sicilian Romance — castles, banditti, and persecuted heroines — helped invent the Gothic novel. Her thrilling mysteries set the pattern for a century. The queen of terror at her best. Trapdoors, veiled nuns, and moonlit castles thrill in her gothic pages.
the-master-of-silence-a-romance: Irving Bacheller's Master of Silence — a romance of a strange, silent man and the mystery he guards — weaves love and intrigue in an old New England setting. The Eben Holden author's storytelling charm never fails. A gentle, engaging romance. A hidden past and a brave girl's love drive this gentle mystery.
the-fighting-chance: Robert W. Chambers' Fighting Chance — a society novel of love, racing, and redemption — shows the King in Yellow author in fashionable mode. His glittering New York world tempts and tests its heroine. A smart, stylish romance of its day. Race tracks and drawing rooms frame her fight for happiness.
o-t-a-danish-romance: Hans Christian Andersen's O.T., a Danish romance of student life in Copenhagen, was his first great success in longer fiction. Love, ambition, and youthful dreams fill its charming pages. Readers who know only the fairy tales will enjoy the novelist. The master storyteller in a more extended form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abstinence: This 1913 reference article on abstinence — the Church's law of fasting from flesh meat. James David O'Neill explains its days and reasons. Fridays and Lent kept the old discipline. A clear guide to a classic practice. Fish on Fridays was the people's mark of faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acceptance: A 1913 entry on acceptance in canon law — the taking up of office or benefice. Richard Burtsell states the formal rules. A bishop's nod could make or break a career. Church law on saying yes. A sealed letter once carried the joyful news.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accomplice: A 1913 entry on the accomplice in moral theology — sharing guilt by counsel or aid. Joseph Delany weighs the degrees of fault. Nine ways to share another's sin. Confessors still use these distinctions. The priest, the lookout, and the driver each bear guilt. Moralists graded every share.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-actual-grace: A 1913 entry on actual grace — God's passing help toward good acts. Joseph Pohle sets out the theology with precision. Every good impulse has heaven behind it. A central doctrine, clearly taught.
